Most nearly mean, underlined phrase or phrase options

items.passage: Testing Andrew Carnegie’s claim that large inheritances discourage heirs from working, economists Douglas Holtz-Eakin, David Joulfaian, and Harvey Rosen examined tax returns and found the probability of leaving the labor force to be ______ the magnitude of the inheritance: single people inheriting more than $150,000 were roughly four times as likely to stop working as those inheriting less than $25,000.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be sensitive to something is to change when it changes. The text compares single individuals “inheriting more than $150,000” with those “inheriting less than $25,000” and finds the first group “roughly four times as likely to stop working,” so the chance of leaving the labor force rose with the size of the inheritance: it was sensitive to that size.

A.why_wrong: Conducive to means helping to bring something about. The text presents the inheritance as what comes first and the decision to stop working as what follows; leaving the labor force did not help produce larger inheritances.

B.why_wrong: Independent of means unaffected by. The text shows the opposite: individuals inheriting more than $150,000 were “roughly four times as likely to stop working” as those inheriting less than $25,000.

D.why_wrong: Incidental to means occurring only as a minor side effect of something. The text does not present leaving the labor force as a minor accompaniment of an inheritance; it shows that the likelihood of leaving rose sharply with the inheritance’s size.

sources.what: NBER working paper 4118 page, Holtz-Eakin, Joulfaian and Rosen, “The Carnegie Conjecture: Some Empirical Evidence” (published QJE 1993): tax return data on labor force behavior before and after inheritances; results consistent with Andrew Carnegie’s century-old assertion that large inheritances decrease labor force participation; a single person with an inheritance over $150,000 is roughly four times more likely to leave the labor force than one with an inheritance below $25,000

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (the two-group comparison shows the likelihood rising with the amount; the blank names that dependence). Raw freq.txt ranks: conducive to 24,104; independent of 3,829; sensitive to 3,071; incidental to 19,860. Band 6: plain key, as in the band-6 B6 models (overshadowed by, a straightforward); the near miss incidental to and the direction reversal conducive to share the key’s register. Carnegie’s claim is given as the source does (an old assertion), with no date. Register pass (resumed run, 2026-10-27): passage reworded toward CB’s density figures with the same facts, key and options; explanation quotes updated to match.

fixes: register: reverted three substitutions from the writer's register pass that added length, not fact (century-old assertion to claim, sizable to large, individuals to people); with items 02 and 03 the hard tier moved from 5.35 to CB's 5.25 chars per word

band7.why: Band 6 by plan. Recounted: conducive to 24,104, independent of 3,829, sensitive to 3,071, incidental to 19,860 (2 of 4 past 10,000, plain key); two steps (a two-group comparison read as a dependence). Strong band 6, like the band-6 B6 models.

items.passage: Starlight filtering through a planet’s atmosphere carries traces of the gases there. Observing the ultrahot giant exoplanet WASP-76b, astronomer David Ehrenreich and colleagues found the planet’s iron absorption to be ______: starlight passing its evening edge, where winds carry gas from the scorching dayside toward the nightside, showed iron vapor, whereas starlight passing its morning edge showed none, suggesting that the iron condenses as it crosses the cooler nightside.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Something asymmetric differs from one side to the other. The text says starlight passing the planet’s “evening edge” revealed iron vapor, “whereas starlight passing its morning edge showed none,” so the iron signal was present on one side of the planet and absent on the other: it was asymmetric.

B.why_wrong: Cyclical means repeating in regular cycles. The text compares the planet’s two edges at one time; it says nothing about the iron signal coming and going in a repeating pattern.

C.why_wrong: Uniform means the same everywhere. The text says the signal appeared at the evening edge but not at the morning edge, which is the opposite of uniform.

D.why_wrong: Spurious means false or not genuine. Nothing suggests the iron signal was an error; the researchers use it to conclude that “the iron condenses as it crosses the cooler nightside.”

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Ehrenreich et al. 2020 (Nature), Nightside condensation of iron in an ultrahot giant exoplanet: asymmetric absorption signature in WASP-76b attributed to neutral iron on the evening (day-to-night) limb, with wind from the hot dayside; no signal near the morning terminator; iron must condense during its journey across the nightside

items.notes: Subject: natural science (astronomy). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (the colon clause gives a difference between two sides in technical terms, evening edge against morning edge; the student must name it with the abstract word). Raw freq.txt ranks: asymmetric unseen (modern word, credited lower by the corrected measure), cyclical unseen, uniform 4,122, spurious 20,718. Band 6, like 3d658a5a (homogeneous from low species richness). The source abstract uses asymmetric; the passage does not. Register pass (resumed run, 2026-10-27): passage reworded toward CB’s density figures with the same facts, key and options; explanation quotes updated to match.

fixes: register: chemical signatures to traces, revealed to showed (twice), toward CB's hard figures; explanation quote updated

band7.why: Band 6 by plan. asymmetric and cyclical are unseen in freq.txt (modern words), uniform 4,122, spurious 20,718; the colon clause gives the two-sided difference in concrete terms and the key names it abstractly, with uniform as the reversal. Strong band 6.

items.subtype: Blank completion: contrast clue (received view, then finding)
items.passage: Although ancient Egyptian texts frequently mention antiu, a substance used in embalming, its chemical identity long remained ______: translators usually rendered the term as “myrrh” or “incense.” Only when Maxime Rageot and colleagues analyzed residues preserved in labeled vessels from an embalming workshop at Saqqara did antiu, as used there, prove to be a mixture based on coniferous oils or tars.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Conjectural means based on guesswork rather than evidence. The text contrasts how often the texts “mention antiu” with what scholars knew of the substance itself: translators “usually rendered the term as ‘myrrh’ or ‘incense,’” and only the residue analysis showed what it was, “a mixture based on coniferous oils or tars.” Until then, antiu’s identity was conjectural.

A.why_wrong: Esoteric means understood only by a small group with special knowledge. The text does not say that a few people knew what antiu was; it says that translators could offer only renderings such as “myrrh” or “incense” until the residues were analyzed.

B.recipe: reversal: the trait of the overturned view (ANT)
B.why_wrong: Incontrovertible means impossible to dispute. The usual renderings of antiu were overturned when the residues proved to be “a mixture based on coniferous oils or tars,” so its identity had not been beyond dispute.

C.why_wrong: Anomalous means departing from what is normal or expected. The text does not present antiu or its identity as unusual; it says only that what the substance actually was had not been established.

band7_moves: concessive frame (Although ... frequently mention) that hides the direction: a much-mentioned substance invites incontrovertible
blank on the received view; the finding comes only in the next sentence (Only when ... prove to be)
near-synonym distractor failing on one feature (esoteric: known to a few, not unknown)

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Rageot et al. 2023 (Nature), Biomolecular analyses enable new insights into ancient Egyptian embalming: organic contents of 31 labeled ceramic vessels from a 26th Dynasty embalming workshop at Saqqara; at Saqqara, antiu, well known from ancient texts and usually translated as ‘myrrh’ or ‘incense,’ refers to a coniferous oils-or-tars-based mixture

items.notes: Subject: social science (archaeology). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (texts often name antiu, yet scholars could only offer differing renderings, and the substance was identified only by the residue study; so its identity had rested on guesswork). Concessive frame: yes. Transferred-sense key: no. Raw freq.txt ranks: esoteric 30,865; incontrovertible 36,669; anomalous 24,259; conjectural 41,050 (4 of 4 past 20,000; mean log10 4.51). Band-5 guard: clear (key is not alone in its band). Kept to the abstract: “as used there” follows its “at Saqqara”; no claim about other sites. Hypothetical, speculative and indeterminate were not offered (each would also fit). Register pass (resumed run, 2026-10-27): passage reworded toward CB’s density figures with the same facts, key and options; explanation quotes updated to match.

fixes: fact: the register pass had turned the abstract's oils-or-tars-based mixture into a mixture of coniferous oils or tars (stronger than the source); restored based on
explanation and why_wrong B quotes updated; band7_moves quote matched to the passage

band7.why: Recounted: esoteric 30,865, incontrovertible 36,669, anomalous 24,259, conjectural 41,050 (4 of 4 past 20,000; combined gate passes on key rank). Concessive frame (Although ... frequently mention) hides the direction, the blank sits on the received view with the finding in the next sentence, and esoteric is a near synonym failing on one feature (known to a few, not unknown). No distractor past 50,000, so check 2 alone would not pass; the set and the frame carry it.

items.passage: In 2014 England’s Chief Medical Officer informed doctors at heavily prescribing practices that their practice prescribed antibiotics at a higher rate than 80% of practices nearby. Michael Hallsworth and colleagues found that these letters reduced prescribing by only about 3%, yet the result can hardly be called ______: over six months, it meant roughly 73,000 fewer antibiotic items.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Trivial means of little importance. The text grants that the letters lowered prescribing “by only about 3%,” but “yet” turns against that impression, and the colon clause gives the reason: over six months, “it meant roughly 73,000 fewer antibiotic items.” So the result can hardly be called trivial.

A.why_wrong: Saying the result “can hardly be called substantial” would agree with “only about 3%,” but “yet” signals the opposite point, and the colon clause stresses how large the total reduction was.

C.why_wrong: Uniform means the same everywhere. The text gives only an overall figure, “roughly 73,000 fewer antibiotic items,” and says nothing about whether the effect differed from practice to practice.

D.why_wrong: Saying the result “can hardly be called measurable” would mean it could not be measured, yet the text reports measured figures: a drop of “about 3%” and “roughly 73,000 fewer antibiotic items.”

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Hallsworth et al. 2016 (Lancet), randomised trial: practices in the top 20% for antibiotic prescribing in their NHS Local Area Team; on 29 September 2014 each GP got a letter from England’s Chief Medical Officer stating that the practice prescribed at a higher rate than 80% of practices in its area; October 2014 to March 2015, 3.3% lower rate, an estimated 73,406 fewer antibiotic items

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral public health). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (the negated frame, then the colon reason that overturns “only about 3%”). Raw freq.txt ranks: substantial 5,835; trivial 6,377; uniform 4,122; measurable 32,842. Band 6, the e7d37666 pattern (two negation flips and one unsupported word). Negation phrased “can hardly be called” to avoid the frequent “far from” and “by no means” frames in our items. Figures rounded from the abstract (3.3%, 73,406). Register pass (resumed run, 2026-10-27): passage reworded toward CB’s density figures with the same facts, key and options; explanation quotes updated to match.

band7.why: Band 6 by plan. substantial 5,835, trivial 6,377, uniform 4,122, measurable 32,842; stated negation (can hardly be called) with two negation-flip distractors, a band-6-only recipe in section 4, and a two-step clue (only about 3%, yet 73,000 items). Strong band 6, not 7.

items.passage:
The following text is from Lucas Malet’s 1906 novel The Far Horizon. Dominic Iglesias has just handed money to a man who refused to thank him for it.

For a while Dominic Iglesias remained standing before the fireplace. He was sad at heart. He had given generously, lavishly, out of proportion, as most persons reckon charitable givings, to his means. But, though the act was in itself good, he was <u>sensible</u> of no responsive warmth, no glow of satisfaction. The transaction left him cold; left him, indeed, a prey to disgust.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “sensible” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “sensible of” means aware of, or cognizant of, in an older sense of sensible. The narrator says that “though the act was in itself good,” Iglesias was sensible “of no responsive warmth, no glow of satisfaction,” and the next sentence confirms that he felt nothing warm: “The transaction left him cold.” So he was cognizant of no warmth: he was aware of feeling none.

A.why_wrong: Sensible can mean showing good judgment, but the sentence is not about whether Iglesias acted wisely; it says what he did or did not feel after giving the money: “no glow of satisfaction.”

B.why_wrong: The scene invites the idea of what Iglesias deserved, since “the act was in itself good,” but the sentence reports his feelings: he felt “no responsive warmth,” and “the transaction left him cold.” It does not say he was undeserving of warmth.

D.why_wrong: Sensible can mean large enough to be noticed, as in a sensible change, but here the word describes Iglesias, a person who feels or fails to feel something, not an amount that can be perceived.

band7_moves: common target in an older, secondary sense (sensible of = cognizant of, aware of), against the everyday sense (wise); key past rank 20,000
two distractors are real senses of the target (Judicious; Appreciable, as in a sensible change), one is a near miss from the scene (Deserving)
dense period prose (as most persons reckon charitable givings) between the reader and the clue

sources.what: Project Gutenberg #8569, Lucas Malet, The Far Horizon (text copied exactly from the paragraph after Iglesias gives the money); publication year 1906 and pseudonym from the Wikipedia article on Lucas Malet (Mary St Leger Kingsley)
Wikipedia, Lucas Malet, list of works: The Far Horizon (1906)
Wiktionary, sensible: archaic sense “Cognizant; having the perception of something; aware of something”

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1906). Key letter C. Ranks in freq.txt (commonest of form and simple stem): Judicious 12,231; Deserving 3,598 (deserve); Cognizant 28,383; Appreciable 22,130 (3 of 4 past 10,000, key past 20,000). Reviewer changed the key from Conscious (1,014) to Cognizant: with Conscious the item failed every band-7 gate in spec/rw/band7/words_in_context.md section 6 and broke the M1 recipe (key a mid-frequency word, as Constraint and Perceptible in the band-7 models, not a plain everyday synonym). Wiktionary glosses the archaic sense of sensible as “Cognizant; having the perception of something; aware of something.” As in 6557f7fc (reserve: Constraint, distractors Modesty, Misgiving, Composure), the difficulty is the polysemy: the everyday sense invites Judicious and the perceptible sense invites Appreciable; Deserving is the one option that also parses (deserving of no warmth) and is ruled out by “the act was in itself good.” The man’s refusal to thank Iglesias is from the preceding page (“I do not even thank you”). Author and work used in no official item; Malet appears nowhere else in our items.

fixes: band 7: key Conscious (rank 1,014) changed to Cognizant (28,383); with Conscious only 2 of 4 options were past 10,000 (Deserving counts as deserve, 3,598, not 13,841 as noted) and the key was a plain everyday word, so it read band 6
explanation and notes rewritten for the new key; dictionary source added

band7.why: After the reviewer's key change (Conscious 1,014 to Cognizant 28,383): Judicious 12,231, Deserving 3,598, Cognizant 28,383, Appreciable 22,130 (3 of 4 past 10,000, key past 20,000; band-5 guard clear, one distractor under 10,000). Common target in a secondary sense against its everyday sense, two distractors are real senses of sensible, and Deserving is the one other option that parses, ruled out by the act being good. As drafted (key Conscious) it failed every section-6 gate and read band 6.

items.passage: Evidence that lunar phases influence the timing of human sleep had long been less than ______. Then, using wrist-worn activity monitors, biologist Leandro Casiraghi and colleagues documented a clear synchronization: in Indigenous Toba/Qom communities in rural Argentina and among participants in a highly urbanized setting in the United States alike, sleep began later and was shorter on nights preceding the full moon.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Conclusive means settling a question beyond doubt. The text says that Casiraghi and colleagues “documented a clear synchronization,” which implies that earlier evidence had not been clear. So that earlier evidence had been less than conclusive.

A.why_wrong: Evidence that was “less than ambiguous” would have been clear already, but the text presents the “clear synchronization” as something the researchers documented only later.

B.why_wrong: Intuitive means easy to grasp or expect. The text does not discuss whether the idea that the moon affects sleep seemed natural; it contrasts earlier evidence with the clear synchronization documented later.

C.why_wrong: Obscure means little known. Nothing in the text suggests the earlier evidence was well known or unknown; the point is that it had not settled the question until the “clear synchronization” was documented.

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Casiraghi et al. 2021 (Science Advances), Moonstruck sleep: evidence for modulation of sleep timing by lunar phases is controversial; wrist actimetry shows clear synchronization of sleep with the lunar cycle from rural Toba/Qom communities in Argentina (with and without electricity) to a highly urbanized setting in the United States; sleep starts later and is shorter on the nights before the full moon

items.notes: Subject: natural science (human sleep, chronobiology). Key letter D. Negator hidden in a comparative (less than), as band-7 notes advise for B5. Raw freq.txt ranks: ambiguous 21,875; intuitive 20,681; obscure 5,213; conclusive 14,802. One negation flip, two unsupported words. The abstract’s “controversial” supports “less than conclusive”; persuasive, consistent and plentiful were not offered (each could be read as fitting). Register pass (resumed run, 2026-10-27): passage reworded toward CB’s density figures with the same facts, key and options; explanation quotes updated to match.

fixes: register: sleep onset was delayed and sleep duration reduced to sleep began later and was shorter (abstract wording read as stilted); medium tier stays at CB's figure

items.passage: Local residents were initially reluctant to ______ architect Itsuko Hasegawa’s competition-winning design for the Shonandai Cultural Center in Japan, concerned that much of the building would be buried below ground level. After numerous discussions with the architect, however, they reconsidered: by the time construction began in late 1989, the design had their unanimous approval.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To endorse a plan is to declare one’s approval of it. The residents were “concerned that much of the building would be buried below ground level,” and only later “reconsidered,” giving the design “their unanimous approval.” So at first they were reluctant to endorse it.

B.why_wrong: To scrutinize is to examine closely. The residents did not avoid examining the design; they worried about it and held “numerous discussions with the architect,” so being reluctant to scrutinize it does not fit.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about who paid for the building; it describes the residents’ worry and their later approval of the design.

D.why_wrong: To publicize is to make widely known. The text concerns whether residents approved of the design, not whether they spread news of it.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Itsuko Hasegawa: she won the 1987 competition for the Shonandai Cultural Centre; the design was initially unpopular with local residents, concerned that the building would be buried below ground level; after many discussions with Hasegawa, when the opening phase of construction began in late 1989 the building was met with unanimous approval

items.notes: Subject: humanities (architecture). Key letter A. Negator hidden in an adjective (reluctant to), like “declines to” in 2.20. Raw freq.txt ranks: endorse 24,916; scrutinize 34,328; finance 9,838; publicize unseen (modern word). One negation flip (scrutinize), two unsupported words. Accept, approve and embrace were not offered. Register pass (resumed run, 2026-10-27): passage reworded toward CB’s density figures with the same facts, key and options; explanation quotes updated to match.

items.passage: Though she was born in Seoul and initially studied composition at Seoul National University, Unsuk Chin is ______ the notion that her music belongs to any specific culture. The composer identifies Bartók, Debussy, and Ligeti as especially significant influences, alongside Balinese gamelan and compositional concepts associated with the medieval French composer Machaut.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be resistant to an idea is to reject or push back against it. “Though” sets Chin’s Korean birth and training against her view of her music, and the next sentence shows why she rejects tying it to one culture: she draws on Bartók, Debussy, Ligeti, “Balinese gamelan,” and “the medieval French composer Machaut.”

A.why_wrong: Being committed to the idea would mean holding that her music belongs to a specific culture. The influences the text lists come from many places and periods, which shows the opposite view.

C.why_wrong: Indifferent to means not caring either way. The text presents a definite position: “Though” she was born and trained in Seoul, she rejects the idea, as her wide range of influences shows.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Chin originated the idea that her music belongs to a specific culture; the text describes her view of that idea, not its source.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Unsuk Chin: born in Seoul, studied composition at Seoul National University, then with Ligeti in Hamburg; does not regard her music as belonging to any specific culture; names Bartók, Stravinsky, Debussy, Webern, Xenakis and Ligeti as important, and Balinese gamelan as influential; uses compositional concepts of medieval composers such as Machaut

items.notes: Subject: humanities (music). Key letter B. Concessive frame (Though) plus examples that span cultures. Raw freq.txt ranks: committed to 3,111; resistant to 55,844 (resist is common; the form is rare in the old corpus); indifferent to 2,479; responsible for 3,178. Skeptical of and opposed to were not offered (each would also fit). Register pass (resumed run, 2026-10-27): passage reworded toward CB’s density figures with the same facts, key and options; explanation quotes updated to match.

items.passage: In 1956 trucking entrepreneur Malcom McLean dispatched the converted tanker Ideal-X from Newark, New Jersey, to Houston, Texas, carrying 58 trailer-sized metal containers, an early demonstration of how ______ containerization could make cargo handling. At the time, loading a ship manually cost $5.86 per ton; loading it with containers cost only about 16 cents per ton.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Economical means costing little. The second sentence gives the comparison: loading a ship manually “cost $5.86 per ton,” while loading it with containers “cost only about 16 cents per ton.” So the voyage showed how economical containerization could make cargo handling.

A.why_wrong: Lucrative means producing a lot of money for the one doing it. The text describes how much loading cost, not how much profit anyone made from handling cargo.

B.why_wrong: Laborious means requiring much work. Containers made loading far cheaper than loading “manually,” so they made cargo handling less laborious, not more.

D.why_wrong: Conspicuous means easily noticed. The text compares the costs of two ways of loading a ship; it says nothing about how visible cargo handling became.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Malcom McLean: on April 26, 1956, the converted tanker Ideal-X sailed from Port Newark, New Jersey, to Houston, Texas, carrying 58 35-foot trailer vans, later termed containers; hand-loading a ship then cost $5.86 a ton, while loading with containers cost only 16 cents a ton

items.notes: Subject: history (business and transport). Key letter C. Raw freq.txt ranks: lucrative 23,461; laborious 12,828; economical 15,405; conspicuous 6,466 (all in one band). Near miss lucrative fails on the feature (profit, not cost). Cheap, affordable, inexpensive and efficient were not offered. Register pass (resumed run, 2026-10-27): passage reworded toward CB’s density figures with the same facts, key and options; explanation quotes updated to match.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Catherine Helen Spence’s 1865 novel Mr. Hogarth’s Will. Two impoverished sisters are lodging with Peggy.

They could not help admiring the wonderful patience which she had with the old man, who was not her own father, but merely the father-in-law of her dead sister. In all little things she <u>gave way to</u> him, but in all great and grave matters she judged and acted for herself, whatever grumbling might follow.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “gave way to” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “gave way to” means yielded to, or let the old man have his way. The sentence sets the phrase against what Peggy did in other matters: “in all great and grave matters she judged and acted for herself.” So in “all little things” she yielded to his wishes, which fits the “wonderful patience” the sisters admire.

B.why_wrong: One thing can give way to another in the sense of being replaced by it, as when winter gives way to spring, but the old man does not take Peggy’s place; the sentence is about whose wishes she follows in “little things.”

C.why_wrong: The mention of “grumbling” may suggest that Peggy found the old man tiresome, but the sisters admire her “wonderful patience” with him, and the sentence describes what she let him decide, not how she felt about him.

D.why_wrong: A floor or a bridge can give way, or collapse, under a weight, but nothing in the text breaks down; the phrase describes how Peggy treated the old man’s wishes in small matters.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg #4224, Catherine Helen Spence, Mr. Hogarth’s Will (two sentences copied exactly from the chapter in which Jane and Elsie Melville, left with little money, first live with Peggy Walker; the middle sentence about snuff and Bible reading trimmed)
Wikipedia, Catherine Helen Spence: her third novel, Mr Hogarth’s Will, published in 1865

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1865, Australian author, set in Scotland). Key letter A. Phrase target with paraphrase options, as in 2.8 (reconcile his mother to). Clue is the contrast inside the sentence (little things vs great and grave matters, where she acted for herself) plus “wonderful patience.” Ranks of head words in freq.txt: yielded 3,438; replaced 5,119; tired 751; collapsed 11,059. Two distractors are other senses of give way to (be replaced by; collapse), one is unsupported. Author and work used in no official item and none of ours.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Rosa Praed’s 1915 novel Lady Bridget in the Never-Never Land.

Presently [Colin McKeith] stood beside her, his tall form, in the well-cut evening suit which always became him best, towering head and shoulders above her small stature. It was always a satisfaction to Lady Bridget, fastidious in such masculine details, that he was <u>particular</u> about his tailoring, and tonight he exhaled the scent of one of Sir Luke Tallant’s excellent cigars.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “particular” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “particular” means careful, or exacting about details. McKeith wears “the well-cut evening suit which always became him best,” and Lady Bridget, herself “fastidious in such masculine details,” is pleased that he takes the same care: he is careful about his tailoring.

A.why_wrong: Particular once meant intimate, as in “a particular friend,” but the sentence is not about a close relationship; it describes how McKeith treats “his tailoring,” the fit and cut of his clothes.

C.why_wrong: Particular can mean exceptional, as in “of particular interest,” and McKeith’s suit is “well-cut,” but the word describes his attitude toward his tailoring, which pleases a woman “fastidious in such masculine details,” not how remarkable he is.

D.why_wrong: Particular can mean individual, as in “each particular case,” but that sense picks out one thing from a group; here the word describes McKeith’s care over “his tailoring.”

sources.what: Project Gutenberg #4051, Mrs. Campbell Praed (Rosa Praed), Lady Bridget in the Never-Never Land (excerpt copied exactly from the terrace scene; [Colin McKeith] replaces “he”)
Wikipedia, Rosa Campbell Praed, list of works: Lady Bridget in the Never-Never Land (1915)

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1915, Australian author). Key letter B. Ranks in freq.txt: careful 1,633; intimate 3,196; exceptional 8,620; individual 2,625 (plain band, key plain as in medium meaning items, 2.3 Characteristic and 2.19 Acquired). All three distractors are real senses of particular. Specific and Detailed were left out because “specific about his tailoring” or “detailed about” could be read as exacting. The next sentence of the novel uses “particularly,” so the excerpt stops before it. Author and work used in no official item and none of ours.

fixes: source line: is from to is adapted from, since [Colin McKeith] replaces he (CB uses adapted in 18 of 21 bracket-substitution excerpts; matches items 15 and 17)

items.passage: The dead horse arum, a Mediterranean plant pollinated by carrion blowflies, generates its own heat. Researchers discovered that this warmth makes part of the plant more ______ to the flies, drawing them to a structure from which they are more likely to crawl into the chamber containing the plant’s flowers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Something attractive draws others toward it. The text says the plant’s warmth ends up “drawing them,” the flies, “to a structure” on the plant, so the heat makes that part of the plant more attractive to the flies.

A.why_wrong: Repellent means driving others away, but the warmth is “drawing” the flies to the structure, not pushing them away.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the heat hides the plant from the flies; the flies are drawn to it.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about whether the flies already know the plant; it says the heat draws them to one of its structures.

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Angioy et al. 2004 (Proc. R. Soc. B), Function of the heater: the dead horse arum revisited: the thermogenic Mediterranean arum Helicodiceros muscivorus attracts carrion blowflies as pollinators; heat produced along the appendix lures the flies to that structure, and flies from the appendix are more prone to enter the trap chamber housing the florets

items.notes: Subject: natural science (botany). Key letter B. Kept to the heat finding (the plant’s carrion smell, a titan-arum style detail, is left out). items.passage: The cursus publicus, a network of roadside stations established by the Roman emperor Augustus, provided fresh animals and lodging to couriers transporting official messages. B.why_wrong: Voluntary means done by choice. The text is about who was allowed to use the stations, not whether anyone chose to.

C.why_wrong: Universal use would mean everyone could use it, but the text says a traveler “needed a permit” and that “most Romans” depended on others to deliver their correspondence.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests the stations were used only at certain times of year.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Flora Annie Steel’s 1896 novel On the Face of the Waters. Tara has just lifted a water pot onto her head and spoken to her brother Soma.

[Soma] was in the undress uniform of a sepoy [soldier], and as he also straightened himself to face the speaker the extraordinary likeness between them in face and figure <u>stamped</u> them as twins.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “stamped” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “stamped” means identified, or showed to be. When Soma faces Tara, “the extraordinary likeness between them in face and figure” makes it plain that they are twins. Their likeness identified them as twins.

A.why_wrong: To stamp can mean to trample something under foot, but no one is stepping on anything; it is the “likeness between them in face and figure” that stamps Tara and Soma as twins.

B.why_wrong: A design can be stamped, or printed, on paper or cloth, but nothing is printed here; the word describes what the likeness between Tara and Soma shows about them.

D.why_wrong: Metal or clay can be stamped, or pressed, into a shape, but the twins are not pressed by anything; their likeness “in face and figure” shows that they are twins.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg #40140, Flora Annie Steel, On the Face of the Waters: A Tale of the Mutiny (sentence copied exactly from the well scene in the opening chapters; [Soma] replaces “He” and a gloss is added for sepoy)
Wikipedia, Flora Annie Steel: On the Face of the Waters (1896)

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1896, set in India). Key letter C. Ranks in freq.txt: identified 8,565; trampled 7,920; printed 3,319; pressed 1,348. All distractors are physical senses of stamp, as all three of 1.19 (drew: Drained, Inspired, Sketched) are other senses; the key is the figurative sense (to mark out as). The novel names the speaker Tara two sentences later, and calls them Tara Devi and Soma Chund, Rajpoots of the same tribe. items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Frank T. Bullen’s 1898 book The Cruise of the “Cachalot.” The narrator is a sailor on a whaling ship.

Nothing could shake [the captain’s] belief in the wonderful numbers of sperm whales to be found on the south coasts of New Zealand, which faith was well warranted, since he had there won from the waves, not only the value of his new ship, but a <u>handsome</u> profit in addition, all in one season.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “handsome” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “handsome” means large. The captain found “wonderful numbers of sperm whales” off New Zealand and in one season earned “not only the value of his new ship, but a handsome profit in addition.” The profit was a large sum on top of the cost of the ship.

A.why_wrong: Handsome often means good-looking when it describes a person, but here it describes a profit, an amount of money, which cannot be good-looking.

B.why_wrong: A handsome room or piece of furniture is elegant, but the text is about how much money the captain made, “the value of his new ship” and more, not about style.

C.why_wrong: A handsome apology is a gracious one, but a profit is not polite or kind; the text stresses its size, earned from “wonderful numbers of sperm whales.”

sources.what: Project Gutenberg #1356, Frank T. Bullen, The Cruise of the “Cachalot” Round the World After Sperm Whales (sentence copied exactly from the chapter on leaving for the Solander grounds; “Still,” dropped and [the captain’s] replaces “his”)
Wikipedia, The Cruise of the Cachalot: an 1898 semi-autobiographical travel narrative by Frank T. Bullen about a whaling voyage from a seaman’s perspective

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Lily Dougall’s 1893 novel What Necessity Knows. Alec Trenholme, a young Englishman who runs a remote railway station in Canada, has just said “good evening” to Saul, a lumberman.

As [Trenholme] spoke, his voice and accent fell upon the air of this wilderness as a rarely pleasant thing to hear. Saul hastily <u>dressed</u> his whiskers with his [rough] left-hand before he answered, but even then, he omitted to return the greeting.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “dressed” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “dressed” means smoothed, or put in order. Before answering the station-master, Saul runs “his [rough] left-hand” over his whiskers to tidy them. He smoothed his whiskers by hand.

B.why_wrong: To dress usually means to put clothes on, but whiskers cannot be clothed; Saul is working on them “with his [rough] left-hand.”

C.why_wrong: A wound can be dressed, or bandaged, but Saul is not hurt; he is tidying his whiskers with his hand before he answers.

D.why_wrong: A dish can be dressed, or garnished, with herbs or sauce, but the text is about a man touching his whiskers, not about food.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg #16398, Lily Dougall, What Necessity Knows (paragraph copied exactly from the chapter in which Saul brings a coffin to Trenholme’s station; [Trenholme] replaces “he” and [rough] replaces “horny”)
Wikipedia, Lily Dougall: Canadian writer, What Necessity Knows (1893), one of her novels set in Canada

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1893, Canadian author, set in Quebec). Key letter A. Ranks in freq.txt: smoothed 6,909; clothed 4,729; bandaged 13,879; garnished absent. All three distractors are other senses of dress (clothe, dress a wound, dress a dish), as in 1.19. The novel itself confirms the sense a few lines later: “Saul smoothed his whiskers again.” “horny” (calloused) was replaced with [rough] so a modern reader is not distracted by it. Garnished (9 letters) keeps the key from being the longest option. Author and work used in no official item and none of ours.

items.passage: The walnut sphinx caterpillar defends itself acoustically: when attacked, it forces air out through a pair of openings in its body, producing a high-pitched whistle. In experiments by Veronica Bura and colleagues, yellow warblers that attacked the caterpillars seemed ______ the whistles, hesitating, jumping back, or diving away, which suggests that the sound deters predators.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be startled by something is to react to it with sudden alarm. The text says the warblers responded to the whistles by “hesitating, jumping back, or diving away,” which shows they were startled by the sound.

A.why_wrong: Birds drawn to the whistles would move toward them, but the warblers were “jumping back, or diving away.”

B.why_wrong: Birds unaffected by the whistles would not react, but the warblers hesitated, jumped back, or dove away.

C.why_wrong: The caterpillar, not the bird, makes the whistle: “it forces air out through a pair of openings in its body.”

items.passage: When the Mexican printmaker José Guadalupe Posada died in 1913, he was largely forgotten and was buried in an unmarked pauper’s grave. His work was later ______ the French-born artist Jean Charlot, who in the 1920s became the first to promote Posada’s cheaply printed illustrations, known as broadsides, as art.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To rediscover something is to find it again after it has been forgotten or overlooked. Posada “was largely forgotten” when he died, and Charlot later “became the first to promote” his illustrations as art. So Posada’s work was rediscovered by Charlot.

A.why_wrong: Charlot did not reject Posada’s work; he “became the first to promote” it as art.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Charlot hired or put Posada’s work to use; the text says he promoted it as art years after Posada died.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no sign that anyone mistook Posada’s work for Charlot’s; it says Charlot promoted Posada’s illustrations.

items.passage: Ruellia ciliatiflora, a flowering plant, launches its tiny disc-shaped seeds from exploding fruits at more than 15 meters per second. Eric Cooper and colleagues discovered that the seeds spin backward during flight, which keeps their thin edges oriented forward. This orientation reduces aerodynamic drag on the seeds, ______ the distance they can travel.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Less drag means less air pushing back against a moving object, so it can go farther. Because the backspin “reduces aerodynamic drag on the seeds,” it ends up increasing the distance they can travel.

A.why_wrong: Reducing drag lets the seeds go farther, so it does not limit the distance they travel.

C.why_wrong: The researchers measured the seeds’ flight, but the reduced drag itself does not record anything; it affects how far the seeds go.

D.why_wrong: Nothing about reduced drag would hide the distance the seeds travel; the text is about how far they can go.

items.passage: Brazilian composer Hermeto Pascoal was known for his ______ choice of instruments. Alongside keyboards and saxophones, he played teapots and children’s toys, and in his composition Música da Lagoa, musicians burble water and play glass bottles while partially submerged in a lagoon.

B.why_wrong: Teapots, toys, and bottles played in a lagoon are not traditional instruments, even though Pascoal also played keyboards and saxophones.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about cost, and teapots, toys, and glass bottles are everyday objects.

D.why_wrong: Pascoal’s choices ranged from keyboards and saxophones to teapots, toys, water, and bottles, a wide rather than limited range.

items.passage: Many of Sol LeWitt’s wall drawings are ______. Executed directly on gallery walls by assistants following the artist’s instructions, they usually last only as long as an exhibition: Wall Drawing #370, for example, was displayed by the Metropolitan Museum of Art from 2014 to 2018 and was subsequently painted over.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

items.passage: In tandem running, an ant that knows the route to a food source guides an inexperienced nestmate there, and the leader takes care not to ______ its follower. When biologist Thomas Richardson and colleagues experimentally removed the follower midway through a run, the leader remained motionless at that location and waited for the follower to return before eventually giving up.

A.why_wrong: The leader shows the follower the way to food, so it is not avoiding teaching the follower; the text describes a leader that waits for its pupil.

B.why_wrong: The text says the leader guides the follower to food, not that it feeds the follower or avoids doing so.

D.why_wrong: The leader goes first and the follower comes after it; nothing suggests the leader ever follows its follower.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Arthur Morrison’s 1894 short story “All That Messuage.” Old Jack Randall and his wife are watching a funeral in a London cemetery.

Ahead of all was the glazed hearse, with attendants in weepers [black mourning bands], and by it, full of the pride of artistry, walked the undertaker himself. The hearse <u>drew up</u> at the chapel door, where the undertaker turned to the right-about and placidly surveyed the movements of his forces.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “drew up” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “drew up” means came to a stop. The hearse has been leading the funeral procession, and it drew up “at the chapel door, where the undertaker turned” around and watched the rest of the procession arrive. The hearse came to a stop at the door.

A.why_wrong: Someone can draw up a bucket from a well, pulling it upward, but the hearse is not lifted; it travels to “the chapel door” and halts there.

C.why_wrong: A lawyer can draw up, or write out, a document, but a hearse does not write anything; the phrase describes the hearse arriving “at the chapel door.”

D.why_wrong: A person can draw himself up, or stand up straight, but a hearse is a vehicle; the text describes where it halts, “at the chapel door.”

Wikipedia, Arthur Morrison: short story collection Tales of Mean Streets (1894)
